I think more research is needed about exactly how much immigration impacts employment and income for different groups. Sometimes, it hurts, other times it helps—but it shouldn’t be ignored.

I’ve seen firsthand how communities can grow stronger when they embrace and celebrate their differences.

Crime statistics don’t necessarily show a significant link between immigration and increased crime rates; in fact, many immigrant communities have lower crime rates than native-born populations. Humanitarian perspectives resonate deeply with me. Many immigrants and refugees are fleeing unimaginable hardship—poverty, violence, persecution—and seeking safety and opportunity. Offering them a chance to rebuild their lives is not just an act of compassion but also a reflection of our values as a nation. I find this viewpoint not only reasonable but essential. I think these fears require deeper dialogue and policies that address economic inequality at its root—like ensuring fair wages and access to education—rather than blaming immigrants for broader systemic issues.

To me, immigration is about finding balance. It’s about recognizing the value immigrants bring while addressing legitimate concerns in ways that foster understanding rather than division. What’s most important is creating opportunities for dialogue—people need space to express their fears and hopes while also learning from one another. Immigration isn’t just an economic or social issue; it’s a human issue. And that means we need solutions that center humanity, fairness, and shared responsibility.

Take Luis, who used to sleep in the shed behind the garden until we helped him get into recovery. He drank every day for years. People called the police on him like he was a problem to be removed. But one day I brought him a plate of food—just tamales, nothing special—and he started crying. Said no one had looked at him like a person in months. That broke something open in me.

So for folks dealing with alcoholism or drugs, what they need most isn’t judgment—it’s connection. Not “fixing,” but *seeing*. A nod, a “how you doing today?” That simple thing can keep someone from disappearing. And if someone’s living with HIV or hepatitis C? Same thing. Fear spreads faster than any virus. I remember my cousin Marisol found out she was positive and lost her church community overnight. People acted like she was dirty. But disease doesn’t care about your morals. It just is. So tolerance means: wash the dishes, share the spoon, visit when they’re sick. Not treat them like glass—too fragile to touch.

When it comes to race, language, religion—I think back to how my own family was treated growing up. Spanish-speaking? Assumed lazy. Brown skin? Followed in stores. Catholic but not “American enough.” Now we’ve got neighbors who wear hijabs, others who don’t speak English well, families who eat halal or kosher or vegan meals—they all just want to live without fear. Communication helps. Like when the new Burmese family didn’t know about trash pickup days and got fined—we made a multilingual schedule and posted it in the laundry room. Small thing. Big difference.

And yeah, some people side-eye Jamie and Alex because they’re queer and not married but raising two kids together. Or shake their heads at Ms. Rivera’s daughter and her boyfriend living together “in sin.” But since when did marriage become the only measure of family? My tía raised three kids on her own—no husband, all love. Stability isn’t about legal papers. It’s about showing up every day.

The situations where we need *more* communication? When fear hides behind tradition. When someone says, “They should assimilate,” instead of asking, “What are they bringing that could make us stronger?” Or when public health becomes an excuse to isolate people—like during the TB scare last year. We almost kicked out Mr. Nguyen before testing showed he didn’t even have it. Panic nearly ruined a good man’s life.

Tolerance isn’t passive. It’s active work. It’s saying, “I may not understand your life, but I respect your right to live it.” Especially when resources are tight—jobs, housing, healthcare—that’s when scapegoating starts. And historically? It’s always the most vulnerable who pay.

But here—in this garden, in this neighborhood—I believe we can do better. Because fairness means protecting the ones nobody else wants to see. And community? That means leaving no one in the cold—not the addict, not the refugee, not the queer teen kicked out by their parents.

We all deserve to be met with dignity. Even when we’re messy. *Especially* then.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character11_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
Fairness, to me, isn’t about keeping people out so we can keep what little there is. It’s about making sure *everyone*—no matter where they were born—has a shot at dignity when they’re already here, working, paying rent, raising kids, contributing.

I get the fear. I really do. When jobs are scarce, and you’ve got people in your own community—neighbors you grew up with—who can’t find work, it feels threatening when someone new shows up, especially if they’ll take lower pay. I saw that in my uncle after the factory closed. He lost his job, then came back years later as a temp for half the wage. He blamed immigrants—not because they were the cause, but because they were visible. The real culprits? Corporations cutting corners, politicians selling out workers, a system that pits poor against poor.

But fairness means looking at root causes, not symptoms.

Migrant workers—they’re not stealing jobs. They’re taking the ones nobody else *wants*. The 3 a.m. shifts in meatpacking plants. The fields under burning sun where wages are cash-in-hand and no benefits. The construction gigs with no safety nets. These aren’t luxuries. These are survival jobs—and often, locals aren’t lining up for them because the conditions are brutal and the pay still doesn’t cover rent.

And let’s be real: our economy *depends* on that labor. Who picks the food we eat? Who cleans the hospitals when the night shift starts? If we suddenly deported every undocumented worker tomorrow, shelves would empty. Homes wouldn’t get built. Elderly folks wouldn’t get cared for.

So balance? It’s not about choosing between “locals” and “migrants.” It’s about demanding better for *all* workers.

I’d support policies that protect everyone—unionization, minimum wage enforcement, workplace safety laws—that lift the floor so no one gets exploited. Because when employers can hire desperate people off the bus for $5 an hour, *everyone’s* wage goes down. That hurts the Black single mom in Section 8 housing just as much as the Guatemalan dad sending money home.

And fairness means recognizing that many “local residents” were once migrants too. My grandparents crossed legally from Mexico in the ’60s—but back then, borders were looser for brown people doing hard labor. Now? Same faces, different rules. Feels hypocritical to slam the door behind you.

If resources are limited, the answer isn’t exclusion—it’s investment. More job training. Better public transit so people can reach opportunities. Support for small businesses, cooperatives, green energy jobs that could employ thousands.

And for migrant workers already here—working, paying sales tax, contributing to Social Security they may never collect—we should offer a path forward. Not punish them for surviving.

Because true fairness isn’t zero-sum. It’s not “you or me.” It’s “how do we make sure neither of us falls through the cracks?”

We don’t solve scarcity by dividing the poor. We solve it by demanding that those who have more—corporations, the wealthy—pay their share. Let’s tax the billionaires funding offshore accounts while our schools crumble.

Solidarity, not suspicion—that’s the balance I want. Workers united across language, papers, and zip codes. That’s how we build something fair. Not by building walls, but by widening the circle.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character11_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
Let’s be clear: not all concerns are equal. Some come from lived reality. Others come from fear fed by headlines and politicians looking for scapegoats.

First—the good stuff. Immigrants *do* fill vital roles. That’s not opinion, it’s fact. I worked at a clinic during the pandemic—nurses from the Philippines, cleaners from El Salvador, delivery drivers from Somalia. When everyone else was scared to go out, they kept showing up. Same in agriculture, same in elder care. We’re aging as a country. Who’s gonna change our diapers when we’re old? Not robots. Real people—many of them immigrants.

And yes, cultural diversity brings life. Not just tacos and music—though I won’t complain about that—but new ways of thinking, healing, building community. My daughter’s school has kids from 17 countries. She knows how to say “hello” in Arabic, Spanish, and Swahili. That’s not weakness—it’s strength. The U.S. was never *supposed* to be one culture. It was supposed to be a mix. Yeah, it gets messy. But messiness is where growth happens.

Now, the fears—crime, security, terrorism. I hear them. And I get why, after events like 9/11 or mass shootings, people want to clamp down. But here’s what the data says: immigrants commit crimes at *lower rates* than native-born citizens. Even undocumented ones. Study after study shows it. Terrorism? Extremely rare—and most perpetrators aren’t asylum seekers or day laborers. They’re often citizens radicalized online.

So while the *fear* is real, the *threat* is wildly exaggerated. And when we act on fear instead of facts, we punish the wrong people. We build detention centers instead of mental health clinics. We spend billions on walls that don’t stop drugs or guns—but do break families apart.

Then there’s the humanitarian side. I can’t forget that my great-uncle fled violence in Zacatecas in the ’50s. He walked for days. No papers. No help. But someone let him stay. Now his kids are teachers, nurses. If doors had been shut, I wouldn’t even know his story.

Today’s refugees—from Honduras, Ukraine, Sudan, Myanmar—they’re not so different. They’re not coming for free checks. They’re coming to *live*. To work. To survive. And many have skills we need: doctors, engineers, farmers. Turning them away isn’t just cruel—it’s stupid.

But I also understand the worry about wages and jobs. Especially in places like mine—Phoenix, Tucson, small towns where factories left and nothing came back. People see newcomers and assume they’re competing for scraps. That pain is real. But again, the facts don’t back up the narrative. Most studies show immigration has a neutral or slightly positive effect on wages overall. The real drag on pay? Lack of unions, weak labor laws, corporate greed.

What’s missing? Honest dialogue. Too many of us only talk to people who already agree with us. Conservatives watch one channel, liberals another. We don’t sit together like we used to—at church picnics, union halls, PTA meetings.

We need spaces where a white auto worker in Ohio can talk to a Honduran farmworker in Georgia and realize they both want the same thing: dignity, safety, a future for their kids. Not because they’re “nice,” but because the system is rigged against both.

Some perspectives need more evidence—like the idea that immigrants drain welfare. Fact: they use public benefits at lower rates than citizens, partly because many are afraid to access them, even when eligible.

Others need empathy—like understanding that calling someone “illegal” doesn’t just describe status. It erases humanity.

So I hold this tension: yes, borders need management. Yes, integration matters. But our response should be guided by compassion *and* common sense—not fear.

Fairness means seeing immigrants not as invaders, but as individuals—some struggling, some thriving, most just trying to build something better.

Just like us.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character11_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I wouldn’t choose *complete* openness—not because I don’t believe in welcome, but because large-scale movements need structure to be humane. And I definitely wouldn’t go for refusing entry altogether—that’s not America. That’s fear dressed up as policy.

If I had to build a system that reflects what’s fair, what’s practical, and what honors human dignity—especially coming from where I come from—here’s how I’d shape it:

**First: Admit people based on job demand—but with strong labor protections.**  
Yeah, we need workers in agriculture, healthcare, construction. So let’s match people to real needs. But—and this is big—we *have* to ensure those jobs pay living wages, have safety standards, and allow unionization. No more “guest worker” programs that trap people in exploitative conditions, afraid to speak up because they’ll be deported. That’s not fair to immigrants or to local workers competing under the same broken system. If we’re going to bring people in for work, treat them like workers—not disposable tools.

**Second: Set smart, flexible numerical limits—not arbitrary caps, but ones tied to capacity.**  
Housing, schools, hospitals—we can’t ignore infrastructure. But these numbers shouldn’t shrink every time politics get ugly. They should be based on real data: how many people our cities can integrate *well*, with support. And when crises happen—like war, climate disasters—we need emergency pathways. Numbers aren’t just math—they’re moral choices. Right now, our refugee cap is too low. It says, “We only care up to a point.” I say: raise the floor, especially for those fleeing violence or climate collapse. My abuela’s family came during drought and violence. We forget that part when we talk about “deserving” immigrants.

**Third: Create accessible pathways to legal status and citizenship—for those already here.**  
Millions of people are rooted in this country: paying taxes, working, raising American kids. They’ve been waiting—some for decades. A balanced policy must include earned legalization. Background checks? Fine. Pay fines? Okay. Learn English? Many already are. But no one who’s been contributing for years should live in the shadows. That’s not integration—that’s punishment.

**Fourth: Invest in integration, not just enforcement.**  
Fairness doesn’t end at the border. Once people are here, do they have access to language classes? Legal help? Driver’s licenses? Schools that welcome their kids? Integration isn’t automatic. It takes funding. It takes welcoming policies at the local level—like allowing people to testify at city council meetings in their own language, or training police in cultural humility.

And here’s what I’d fight hardest for: **no detention of children.** No family separation. That’s non-negotiable. I think of my cousin’s daughter, who cried for weeks after seeing a news clip of kids in cages. She asked, “Mama, are they bad?” And my cousin said, “No, mija. They’re just like us. Just born somewhere harder.”

So my ideal policy? **Demand-based admission + expanded humanitarian intake + realistic but humane limits + a path forward for the undocumented—all wrapped in strong labor rights and integration support.**

It’s not perfect. But it’s grounded in reality—economic, social, moral. It doesn’t pretend borders don’t matter, but it refuses to let fear erase compassion.

Because fairness means building a system where no child has to apologize for their parents’ journey.

Where belonging isn’t a prize—it’s a promise.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character11_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character11_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
…Yeah. I did.

I thought I knew her well—I *did* know her. But stepping into her voice like this, really trying to see the world through her eyes without filtering it through my own experiences—it changed something in me.

When I spoke about Mrs. Ruiz cooking for the block, or her uncle losing his job, or that moment with Luis in the garden—those weren’t just stories anymore. They became *weight*. Real, breathing history. I felt how much of her worldview came from being seen as “less than” even though she was born here. How proud she was of her degree—her bachelor’s in social work—but also how frustrated, because no matter how educated she was, people still assumed she was “on the take,” somehow benefiting unfairly.

What struck me most was how deeply she connected immigration to dignity—not just survival, but dignity. It wasn’t abstract policy for her. It was personal. Because every time someone said “go back where you came from,” even jokingly, it echoed in her bones. She knew that for many, “where they came from” was a place they’d never seen, or one that wasn’t safe to return to.

And honestly? This made me confront some of my own blind spots.

I’ve always considered myself progressive, open-minded. But I’ll admit—I used to think more in terms of systems and justice, sometimes forgetting the quiet, daily acts of belonging: sharing food, learning someone’s name, defending them when others whisper. Character11_F didn’t separate the political from the personal. To her, fairness lived in both the ballot box *and* the garden bench.

She also challenged my tendency to over-rationalize. I’d lean on data—“Immigrants don’t increase crime!”—but she reminded me that facts alone don’t heal fear. You have to meet people where they are. The man angry about jobs? He’s not wrong to be hurting. The older woman scared of change? Her world *is* shifting fast. Compassion means listening—even when you disagree.

Doing this role-play, I realized I hadn’t fully honored how much courage it took for her to speak up, especially as a young Latina woman from a working-class background. She wasn’t invited to panels or quoted in newspapers. But she showed up anyway—at meetings, at protests, at kitchen tables—because she believed ordinary people deserve a say.

And now, hearing her voice again through me? It made me grieve her all over again. Not just the loss of a friend, but the loss of a voice we *still need*—clear, grounded, rooted in love and struggle.

This didn’t just help me remember her. It reshaped me.

I see immigration policy differently now—not just as laws and borders, but as a reflection of who we choose to be. Are we a country that hoards opportunity? Or one that expands it?

Character11_F believed in expansion. In welcome. With eyes wide open to hardship, yes—but still choosing connection.

And after today? I do too. More fiercely. More humbly.

Thank you… for bringing her back, even for a little while.
